summary: Sets out high-level requirements for an incident data format that CSIRTs can use to describe, archive, and exchange information about security incidents. The work was done through TERENA. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Security teams need a common form to report what went wrong so they can share notes. This lists what that form should be able to do.

subtitle: High-level requirements for a standard incident data exchange format between security teams.

tldr.problem: When security incidents span multiple organizations and countries, incident response teams need a common language to describe what happened, who was affected, and what actions were taken. Without a standard format, teams cannot efficiently share and coordinate on investigations.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines functional and technical requirements for IODEF (Incident Object Description and Exchange Format), which will allow CSIRTs to describe incidents in a structured, machine-readable way that supports filtering, aggregation, archiving, and secure exchange.
tldr.outcome: The requirements paved the way for IODEF implementations that enable teams to cooperate on distributed, cross-border incidents using a common vocabulary and data model.

facts.label: Required address types
facts.value: IPv4, IPv6, DNS names, MAC, ATM addresses

facts.label: Date/time requirement
facts.value: Must support dates beyond 2038 (no Unix time limitation)

today: RFC 3067 is Informational and defines the requirements that guided the development of IODEF, which has become the standard format for incident reporting and exchange in international cybersecurity coordination. The requirements remain current as CSIRTs continue to use IODEF-based systems for cross-organizational incident response.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 3067 defines requirements for the Incident Object Description and Exchange Format (IODEF), a standard format for security teams called CSIRTs (Computer Security Incident Response Teams) to describe, archive, and exchange incident information. The document arose from attempts to establish cooperation among advanced CSIRTs in Europe and the FIRST community.

The RFC focuses on a clear problem: computer incidents are increasingly distributed and international, often crossing organizational and national borders. A CSIRT in one country may need to communicate with CSIRTs in others about the same incident. Without a standard format, teams waste effort translating between incompatible reporting systems, delaying response and investigation.

The requirements balance two needs: human readability (CSIRTs still create incident reports by hand) and machine processing (automated tools should be able to parse, filter, and correlate incidents). The RFC assumes IODEF will be created by humans and transmitted via standard channels like email or HTTP, but processed automatically by incident handling systems.
sections.eli5: Security teams around the world need to write down incident details the same way so they can swap notes quickly, even if they speak different languages or use different tools.

sections.title: Core Incident Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC defines essential terms for incident reporting:

  • Attack: An assault on system security derived from an intelligent threat, either active or passive, by insider or outsider.
  • Attacker: The individual attempting attacks, described in IODEF by network ID, organization, and location.
  • CSIRT: The Computer Security Incident Response Team handling the incident and creating the incident description.
  • Damage: Intended or unintended consequences of an attack on the targeted system or service.
  • Event: Any observable occurrence in a system or network that results in an alert, such as three failed logins in 10 seconds.
  • Evidence: Information supporting conclusions about an event, including IDS data, syslog entries, kernel statistics, memory dumps. Must be stored securely with chain-of-custody documentation.
  • Incident: A security event involving a security violation, either a single attack or related attacks distinguished by method, attacker identity, victims, or timing.
  • Vulnerability: A flaw or weakness that could be exploited to violate the system's security policy.

These definitions form the basis for a common vocabulary across all IODEF implementations.
sections.eli5: An incident is when someone attacks, the attack is what they do, evidence is the proof of what happened, and a vulnerability is a hole they exploited.

sections.title: Format and Content Requirements
sections.content:
IODEF descriptions must support full internationalization, allowing operators to read reports in local languages with localized date/time formats. The character set must be ISO/IEC 10646-1 (Unicode) encoded as UTF-8 to support non-Latin characters.

The format must be modular to support filtering and aggregation: some fields may be removed for privacy, external evidence may be referenced by URL, and different CSIRT departments may need different subsets of the data.

The root incident element must include a unique identifier, purpose (alert, handling, archiving, reporting, or statistics) and default permission level, which can then be applied at the element level. Sensitive elements such as passwords, forensic data, or organizational identifiers must be marked with access restriction attributes.

Core content must include: the attack type (from a standardized list or new implementation-specific type), attacker and victim descriptions (minimum IP/DNS names, extended to include organizations), creator identity (the CSIRT handling it), references to advisories (CERT/CC, CVE), a detailed attack description, optional evidence, impact assessment (from a standardized list or free text), confidence level, and a complete audit trail of actions taken by all CSIRTs involved.

Time must be reported in local time with UTC offset, using a date format that avoids Y2K issues and can represent dates past 2038. The granularity of time need not be specified, allowing different systems to provide seconds, milliseconds, or coarser values as available.
sections.eli5: An incident report needs: who wrote it, what happened, who attacked, who was hit, what we did about it, when, and what the impact was. Different parts can be kept secret or shared as needed.

sections.title: Security, Extensibility, and Exchange
sections.content:
IODEF descriptions may contain sensitive data such as passwords, forensic evidence, or personally identifiable information. The format must support confidentiality (multiple encryption algorithms, adaptable to different environments), integrity (mechanisms to prevent malicious changes), and authenticity and non-repudiation (proving who created the incident report and preventing creators from denying authorship).

The format must be extensible to accommodate new incident handling tools, integration with related standards (such as IDEF for Intrusion Detection or future evidence custody formats), and implementation-specific needs. Implementers must clearly indicate how to interpret any extensions.

Exchange of incident information typically occurs via human-initiated communication: email, HTTP/WWW, or LDAP, with authorization from an operator or CSIRT manager. Communications security is applied separately according to local policy and is outside IODEF's scope. The format must reference and reuse previously published RFCs and standards wherever possible to ensure compatibility with existing security infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Incident reports must be secret and signed so no one can fake them or spy on them. Teams can add their own custom fields if needed, but they must say what the new fields mean.

viz.caption: Required Elements in an Incident Report

items.title: Identifier
items.text: Unique ID including CSIRT name and classification.

items.title: Attacker
items.text: Network ID, organization, and location of the attack source.

items.title: Victim
items.text: Network ID, organization, and location of the target.

items.title: Attack Type
items.text: From a standard list, or new type if not yet standardized.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: IDS alerts, log files, or links to forensic data.

items.title: Impact
items.text: Financial, operational, or security impact on victim.
